seo.title: Karmic tail 3 13 19 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 13 19 compatibility: why Death stands between The Empress and The Sun, how the tail is built, and what the tale of Savitri knows about it.

title: The couple's karmic tail 3-13-19: The Empress, Death and The Sun
short: The karmic tail 3-13-19 turns up in roughly one couple in 129: The Empress at the entry, Death in the middle, The Sun as the main task. It looks like a story with a bad middle, but the answer lies elsewhere. Death here is the end of an old form of life, and the two go through it together. The real difficulty hides in The Sun: one partner knows and keeps quiet, protects and smiles, while the other lives on knowing nothing. The couple's task is to bring what one of them knows into a light both can see by.

sections.h2: A tale that lays out the three cards in order
paragraphs: The story of Savitri and Satyavan sits in the Forest Book of the Mahabharata (chapters 277–283 in the critical edition). The sage Markandeya tells it to King Yudhishthira as consolation, and it opens with a childless king, Aswapati. For eighteen years he keeps strict vows and makes offerings while reciting the Savitri — the famous prayer to the solar god Savitr. The goddess of that verse rises from his fire and promises him a daughter "of great energy". The girl is named Savitri.

She grows up so bright that no one asks for her hand: the text says that, "overpowered by her energy, none could wed" her. Her father sends her to choose a husband herself. Savitri travels from one forest hermitage to the next and chooses Satyavan, son of a blind king whom an enemy has driven from his throne. The sage Narada praises the young man without pause and then names the one defect that outweighs all his virtues: "Within a year from this day, Satyavan, endued with a short life will cast off his body!" Savitri does not change her choice. Then come the wedding, a year in the hermitage, the appointed day, Yama the god of death with his noose, a conversation on the move, five boons and a journey home by night.
The three acts follow the order of the cards:

ul: **The Empress:** eighteen years of praying for offspring, then a wedding and a home in the forest, where the new daughter-in-law tends and shelters everyone;
**Death:** a year counted day by day, and a god who comes for the husband in person;
**The Sun:** the road back through the night, the truth told by the fire, and the sunrise that brings good news to the hermitage.

paragraphs: The Sun in this story does not have to be read between the lines — it is named outright. Savitri bears the name of the solar verse. Narada says that "in energy Satyavan is like unto the sun"; the Sanskrit names Vivasvat, the Sun himself. Yama appears "effulgent as the Sun", and Savitri addresses him as the son of Vivasvat. In this myth Death is the son of the Sun. The middle of the tail and its main task are father and son.
Quotations from the Mahabharata here and below follow K. M. Ganguli's English translation (1883–1896), checked against the Sanskrit.

sections.h2: The evidence in the numbers: why the middle is Death and not The Fool
paragraphs: The first oddity is plain to see. In a personal chart the middle of the tail comes from its two ends: entry plus main task. If 3-13-19 belonged to one person, the card between The Empress and The Sun would be 3 + 19 = 22 — The Fool, a light step into the unknown. No person has such a tail. In a couple, each point is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, and the middle is built from the partners' middles. In place of the light step stands Death — a step after which the old life does not come back.

The second clue is the make-up. Running every possible date gives a single recipe: one partner has the personal tail 15-5-8, the other 15-8-11, and this holds for **100%** of such couples. The sums go point by point:

ul: entry: 15 + 15 = 30 → 3, The Empress made of two Devils;
middle: 5 + 8 = 13, Death made of one partner's Hierophant and the other's Justice;
main task: 8 + 11 = 19, The Sun made of Justice and Strength.

paragraphs: Personal tails are read by their own rules, and their meanings do not carry over into the couple's tail. But the pattern of the sums is evidence, and the tale answers each line. In Waite's list, The Devil is also "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". Savitri's story begins with exactly that: a prediction. The Hierophant and Justice are teaching and law; we will come back to them when Savitri starts talking to Death. And The Sun is made of Justice and Strength — of honest reckoning and gentle firmness. These, not heroics, are what bring her husband back.
The third clue is the centre. In every such couple, without exception, the atmosphere inside the couple is 11, Strength: the two personal centres are always 7 and 4. It gets a chapter of its own.
In frequency the tail sits mid-table: about one couple in 129 (0.778%), 46th of the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a house where nobody asks for anything (3 · The Empress)
paragraphs: The Empress at the entry is what the couple wants together. Here it is a home where things grow: children or a shared business, a garden or a kitchen where someone is always eating. The common language of such couples is care given with the hands: to feed, to fix, to fetch, to drive someone somewhere. The couple enters the task through this wish, and the same wish becomes resistance.

The tale shows exactly how. After the wedding Savitri's father leaves, and that very day she puts off all her ornaments and clothes herself in bark, as people live in a hermitage. She dresses and tends her mother-in-law; she gratifies her father-in-law, in Ganguli's words, "by worshipping him as a god and controlling her speech"; she pleases her husband "by her honeyed speeches, her skill in every kind of work" and "the indications of her love in private". A model household. And a year later the father-in-law says something easy to miss: "Since Savitri hath been bestowed by her father as my daughter-in-law, I do not remember that she hath ever spoken any words couching a request." Her first request in a year comes on the day her husband is to die: to let her go into the forest with him.

In Waite, The Empress is "fruitfulness, action, initiative", followed at once by "the unknown, clandestine". In this house the secret has lived there from the first day. Waite is sharper still in his account of the symbolism: The Empress is "the outer sense of the Word", but "she does not herself carry its interpretation". The Empress speaks through deeds. Couples with this entry understand each other for years through a laid table, and put the words off.

The other hero has an Empress of his own — his parents'. Satyavan lives in his father and mother's hermitage. The moment he wakes from death and sees that night has fallen, he thinks not of what has happened to him but of his parents: "Even before it is twilight my mother confineth me within the asylum"; more than once the old couple wept to him at night that he was "the crutch of these blind ones" and that on him "doth perpetuity of our race depend", and without them he will not live. The couple lives in someone else's house, by its clock.

Among the tasks of this energy, Lisovskaya names getting out from under the influence of the mother and the wider family and leaving infantility behind; among her advice to the couple is to speak about wishes directly. In life it shows in small things. Sunday lunches at the parents' that cannot be missed. A shared country house where the couple has no say. A family business that feeds everyone except its owners. And a partner who never asks for anything, next to a partner who never notices: the couple's wish is shared, but the requests belong to no one.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a year lived as a farewell (13 · Death)
paragraphs: The middle of the couple's tail is how the couple walks the path from the wish to the task. This is our reading: the book gives the point no meaning of its own, and Lisovskaya treats it as an addition to the main task. With Death the path runs through endings: something keeps ending so that something else can grow.

Savitri walks this path alone. "The words spoken by Narada were present night and day" in her mind. She counts the days, and three days before the appointed one she takes a vow to fast for three nights. Her father-in-law begs her to spare herself, and she begins "to look (lean) like a wooden doll". On the appointed morning she goes into the forest with her husband, "in seeming smiles although her heart was racked with grief". The woods ring with peacocks, and Satyavan leads her on, pointing: "Behold these rivers of sacred currents and these excellent trees decked with flowers!" She has not left the hermitage for almost a year. And she looks at her husband and, the text says, "considered her husband as already dead".

This is the minus of Death in the middle: the ending is lived in advance, and inside one head. One partner has already said goodbye to the old life — to a city, a job, the parents' house, the role of newlyweds — while the other is still pointing out the flowers. Waite writes of Death: "The veil or mask of life is perpetuated in change." Savitri's smile on the way to the forest is that mask.

Lisovskaya lists tasks under the thirteenth energy that read like a list of endings: to separate from the parents, to buy a home of one's own, to move, to accept a partner unlike the previous one, to go through separations and crises as a test, to see one's own mistakes and not only the other's. In the minus there are emotional swings, when there is so much change that the other has nothing to lean on, and attempts to remake the partner. In the plus there is a couple who accept each other's past and move on, take changes in the partner easily and are living proof that life goes on after hard times.

Wen writes that Death "assuages the tendency in human nature to resist change" and calls it "a call to let go of the present and move on". Resistance here comes in two kinds: clinging to the old form with all one's strength, or burying it silently without saying a word to the other.

sections.h2: Death talked round: seven steps and the King of Dharma
paragraphs: Then the tale does something no one expects from a story about death. Satyavan is chopping wood when his head starts to split; he lays it in his wife's lap. Yama appears — in yellow robes, noose in hand, "effulgent as the Sun". "By main force" he pulls out of the body a person "of the measure of the thumb" and sets off to the south. Savitri follows.

Yama tells her to turn back and perform the funeral rites. She answers: "Whither my husband is being carried, or whither he goeth of his own accord, I will follow him thither. This is the eternal custom." And she adds: "It hath been declared by wise men endued with true knowledge that by walking only seven paces with another, one contracteth a friendship with one's companion." The seven steps are the **saptapadi**, the heart of the Hindu wedding: in the old ritual manuals, at the seventh step the groom says to the bride, "Be friend with seven steps". Under India's Hindu Marriage Act of 1955, a marriage that includes this rite "becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken". Savitri walks the wedding steps with Death and calls it friendship. She does not fight and does not beg — she walks alongside and talks.

Every speech of hers pleases Yama, and for each he grants a boon — anything but her husband's life. One of the speeches runs: "Thou art the powerful son of Vivaswat. It is for this that thou art called Vaivaswata by the wise. And, O lord, since thou dealest out equal law unto all created things, thou hast been designated the lord of justice!" Dharmaraja, the King of Dharma, is Yama's standing title.

Now back to the sum. This couple's Death is made of one partner's Hierophant and the other's Justice. Waite's divinatory list for The Hierophant begins "marriage, alliance"; the list for Justice begins "equity, rightness, probity". Teaching and law. In the tale, Death is the King of Dharma, and Savitri's weapon is the formula "the wise have declared". She defeats Death with its own law, set out in the language of teachers.

For the couple this is an important hint. Endings in such a union do not strike like lightning: they have rules, and they can be talked to — what ends, what stays, on what terms, by when. The mistake is to treat the middle as a disaster to be fought or got through in secret. The strong move is to walk next to the ending and speak to it aloud, together.

sections.h2: The key was at the entry: a boon Death could not keep
paragraphs: There are five boons, and their order matters. First Savitri asks for her father-in-law's sight, that he may "become strong 'like either fire or the Sun!'" Then for his kingdom back. Then for a hundred sons for her own father. The fourth boon is a hundred sons for herself: "Both of me and Satyavan's loins, begotten by both of us, let there be a century of sons." Yama agrees — and walks into a trap. Savitri says: "Thou thyself hast bestowed on me the boon, namely, of a century of sons; yet thou takest away my husband!… May Satyavan be restored to life, for by that thy words will be made true." The King of Dharma cannot break the law. "With cheerful heart" he unties his noose.

Nobody tricks Death here. It is bound by its own word, and that word was given to The Empress's wish — to fruitfulness, to lineage, to a shared future. **The entry of the tail turns out to be the key to its middle.** The wish the couple started from is neither ornament nor naivety: it is the argument that carries the two of them through the end.

A couple with the tail 3-13-19 recognises this move in its own life. When something ends — a move, a change of job, leaving the parents' house, the end of the first and easiest season — what holds them is not the attempt to keep everything as it was. What holds them is the shared wish said aloud: this is what we are growing, and it needs both of us. A wish with room for both is stronger than any ending. A wish one partner carries in silence holds no one.

sections.h2: Main task: "Wherefore didst thou not awake me?" (19 · The Sun)
paragraphs: The couple's main task is read mainly through its minus — through what does not work. And the tale shows that minus with merciless precision.

Satyavan opens his eyes and looks at his wife "like one come home after a sojourn in a strange land". His first words: "Alas, I have slept long! Wherefore didst thou not awake me? And where is that same sable person that was dragging me away?" Savitri replies: "The night deepens. I shall, O prince, relate everything unto thee on the morrow." At the hermitage the ascetics ask why the pair came back so late. Satyavan explains: his head ached and he fell into a deep sleep — "This is all that I remember… There is no other reason for this." Satyavan means "the one who has truth"; the Brahmanas named him so because "his father speaketh the truth and his mother also is truthful in her speech". And here the man named for truth tells his own story without one false word and without knowing its main point. He is the only one who does not know he was saved.

This is the minus of The Sun in a couple. One partner knows, decides and rescues; the other lives in an ignorance created for them out of love. Among the couple's tasks under the nineteenth energy, Lisovskaya names the inability to talk about problems, holding back feelings, over-protection, inflated expectations and claiming the partner's victories. In life it looks ordinary. One partner learns about a debt, a redundancy, the parents' decision to sell the house — and "sorts it out alone". The other finds out later, from the bank, from friends, from a mother-in-law. The story of the rescue belongs to one person, and it has a single narrator. The rescuer gets a year of loneliness; the rescued gets the role of a child protected from the truth.

Tradition has remembered the tale in just this way. In the Indian month of Jyeshtha, married women keep the Vat Savitri fast: they walk around a banyan tree, winding a thread about it, and pray for their husbands' long life. In the folk version of the tale, it all happened under a banyan. What survives of the whole story is the vow of one partner for the other. The Mahabharata itself ends differently.

Savitri has a formula of her own, spoken back in front of Narada, when her father urged her to choose someone else: "Having first settled a thing mentally, it is expressed in words, and then it is carried out into practice." With the prophecy she walked this path with a gap. She settled it in her mind and carried it out in deeds — the vow, the walk into the forest, the conversation with Death — but put off the words to her husband for a year and one more night. The main task of the tail is the missing middle of her formula: the word.

And the word is spoken. By the fire, in front of everyone, the ascetic Gautama says: "O Savitri, I know thee to be like the goddess Savitri herself in splendour… If it should not be kept a secret, do thou unfold it unto us!" She answers: "I have no secret to keep. Listen to the truth then!" — and tells them everything, from Narada's words to the five boons. On the road behind Yama she had said one more thing: "Verily it is the righteous who by their truth make the Sun move in the heaven." In the tale the Sun rises after the truth is told, not before: in the morning people come to the hermitage with the news that the kingdom has been restored.

Of The Sun reversed, Wen writes: "Success will be obfuscated." The couple's victory over its endings is real, but while only one of them knows about it, it stays in shadow. The Sun in this couple's task is not brightness or success on show, but a light in which both can be seen.

In the tale the wife knows and the husband sleeps. In a living couple, the role of Savitri goes to whoever found out first, and the roles change from one occasion to the next. Gender decides nothing here.

sections.h2: The strong version: the axe on her shoulder, the road in his memory
paragraphs: The truest scene in the tale is the way back, and it almost never makes it into retellings. Night, jackals howling. Savitri suggests waiting until morning by the fire from a burning dead tree. Satyavan is desperate to get back to his parents. So she ties up her hair, raises her husband, places his left arm on her left shoulder, holds him with her right arm and carries his axe. And he says: "By virtue of habit, the (forest) paths are known to me. And further, by the light of the moon between the trees, I can see them… Near that tract overgrown with Palasa tree, the way diverges into two. Do thou proceed along the path that lies to the north of it."

Each has a light of their own: she has the strength, he has the knowledge of the road. Neither leads the other all the way. This is the plus of The Sun in a couple: in Lisovskaya, respect, each successful in their own work, the partner's growth pushing one's own growth, honesty. Wen writes that in questions of love The Sun "could suggest a power couple". It is powerful not because one of them is.
What changes the script:

ul: bad news on the same day, even in a single sentence, without a ready-made solution;
the one who protects asks "do you want to know?" instead of deciding for the other;
a shared success told in two voices, even if one of them did more of the work;
telling the end of a form from the end of the union: saying aloud what is ending and what stays;
putting the shared wish into words, not only into deeds: it is what holds in the middle;
checking now and then what one of the two has long stopped asking for.

sections.h2: The atmosphere inside the couple: Strength, without exception (11)
paragraphs: The centre of the couple is the same for every pair with the tail 3-13-19 — 11, Strength. This is the atmosphere inside the couple, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. And it is always built from the same personal centres: 7 and 4, The Chariot and The Emperor.

Wen separates two cards of strength. The Chariot is the strength that masters the world around; Strength is the strength that masters the self. The sum is telling: two strengths turned outward — victory and power — give the couple a strength turned inward. Wen writes, "Compassion is strength", and adds that here one "cannot use brute force to exercise will over others" — only "gentle, subtle influence". Waite's account of the symbolism has a line about "the strength which resides in contemplation".

In the tale only Yama uses force: "by main force" he pulls the soul from the body. Savitri never uses force once. She has a firm mind — Narada tells her father so: "the heart of thy daughter Savitri wavereth not" — and a way of speaking that leaves Death pleased. Lisovskaya sees both plus and minus in Strength as the atmosphere of a couple. In the plus, the two sense finely what the other needs and charge each other up. In the minus, each has their own truth, and there is a struggle for leadership.

This atmosphere has a shadow, and it leads straight to the main task. Reversed, Waite's Strength is "despotism, abuse of power, weakness, discord". Gentle firmness that decides for two is the same despotism, only quiet. The year when Savitri alone knew the date is the same Strength turned towards its shadow: out of love, but on behalf of two.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a choice made once (6 · The Lovers in 85.6%)
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, one more answer to why the two met. In 85.6% of couples with this tail, The Lovers stand here, 6.

Savitri states the value of The Lovers herself, answering her father after the prophecy: "Indeed, with a life short or long, possessed of virtues or bereft of them, I have, for once, selected my husband. Twice I shall not select." In Waite, The Lovers are "attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome". The trial is in the list, and it is already behind them. In Lisovskaya, the atmosphere of The Lovers in the plus is sincerity, trust and no secrets. The couple's values answer its main task by themselves: a choice made once has no room for a secret inside it.

In 14.4% of couples the values card is The Devil, 15. Then the same story reads through another line of Savitri's: "Without my husband, I do not wish for happiness. Without my husband, I do not wish for heaven itself. Without my husband, I do not wish for prosperity." Devotion that leaves nothing but the other person is no longer a choice but a noose. Such couples do well to remember that in the tale Yama untied his noose himself, and gladly.

sections.h2: Waite: a mask, a chain of flowers and two children by a wall
paragraphs: The drawings of the classic Waite–Smith deck finish the tale where it falls silent.

On Waite's Strength a woman is closing a lion's jaws, and the lion is "being led by a chain of flowers". Waite reads the chain as "the sweet yoke and the light burden". The tale of Savitri has two kinds of bond: Yama's noose, which tightens, and a union that holds without tightening. The atmosphere of this couple is a chain of flowers, not a noose.

On Waite's Death there is a rider with a banner, and on the horizon, between two pillars, the sun shines. Here Death and The Sun are neighbours both in the picture and in the myth, where Death is the son of the Sun.

Waite's Sun is a naked child on a white horse with a red standard. But Waite himself reminds us that older cards were drawn differently: beneath the dog-star there is a wall suggesting an enclosure, "as it might be, a walled garden", and in it two children "gambolling, or running hand in hand". The old Sun has two figures. For a couple's tail no picture could be more exact: the main task is two people under one light, not one person carrying the light for both.

And a coincidence worth calling a coincidence. Narada says that as a boy Satyavan "used to make horses of clay. And he used also to draw pictures of horses", and so he was nicknamed Chitraswa, "he of the painted horses". On Waite's Sun the child rides a horse.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 3-13-19 tail from two dates
paragraphs: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal charts, folded down to 22. The couple's tail is read in order: entry to the task, middle, main task.

An example: a couple born on 14.08.1975 and 14.10.1976. The first partner's day is 14, month 8, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task: 14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8. Centre: 14 + 8 + 22 + 8 = 52 → 7. Entry to the tail: 8 + 7 = 15. Middle: 8 + 15 = 23 → 5. Personal tail: 15-5-8.

The second partner's day is 14, month 10, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task: 14 + 10 + 5 = 29 → 11. Centre: 14 + 10 + 5 + 11 = 40 → 4. Entry to the tail: 11 + 4 = 15. Middle: 11 + 15 = 26 → 8. Personal tail: 15-8-11.
Now add the matching points:

The atmosphere inside the couple is 7 + 4 = 11, Strength; this pair's values card is 6, The Lovers. The shared birthday, the 14th, is a coincidence of the example: in 95% of couples with this tail the partners' day numbers differ.
The couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends. Adding the entry and the main task gives 3 + 19 = 22, while the couple's tail has 13.

ul: **3 · The Empress — entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a home where things grow — children, a garden, a shared business, a laid table. Their common language is care. The same care turns into resistance when it becomes silent service and life by the rules of someone else's house.

**13 · Death — middle of the task.** How the couple moves from the wish to the task: through endings. The parents' house, old roles, plans that have run their course. What ends is a form, not the union.
**19 · The Sun — main task.** A light in which both can be seen: talking about hard things in time, not rescuing each other in secret, not splitting the couple into a hero and the one who was saved.

intro: There is a story in the Indian epic where these three cards stand in exactly this order. It has been retold for nearly two thousand years, and its key question is asked not by a sage or a god, but by a husband who has just come back from the dead: "Wherefore didst thou not awake me?"

faq.q: Is the 3-13-19 tail in compatibility a bad sign?
faq.a: No. Death in the middle of a couple's tail predicts no break-up or misfortune and names no dates. It is the card of a form coming to an end: the parents' house, old roles, plans that have run their course. The tail describes tasks through which the couple grows, not events that will happen to it.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal chart?
faq.a: In a personal chart the middle of the tail is the folded sum of the entry and the main task, so with an entry of 3 and a task of 19 it is always 22. In a couple, the middle is built from the two partners' middles, which is why Death can stand between The Empress and The Sun.

faq.q: If a couple has the 3-13-19 tail, what are the partners' personal tails?
faq.a: Always the same: one has 15-5-8, the other 15-8-11. Running every date finds no other combination. The personal tails are still read by their own rules, and the couple's tail separately, as the shared task of the two.

faq.q: Who in the couple is Savitri, and who is Satyavan?
faq.a: Either of the two. The role of the one who knows and protects goes to whichever partner learns about the hard thing first, and across a couple's history it passes back and forth. Gender does not assign the roles.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. The numbers 3, 13 and 19 make only one couple tail, 3-13-19: The Empress at the entry, Death in the middle, The Sun as the main task.

report: A husband who has just come back from the dead asks his wife, before anything else: "Wherefore didst thou not awake me?" The scene comes from the tale of Savitri in the Mahabharata, and the whole 3-13-19 tail is in it. Death is not the most dangerous thing here. report: For every speech Yama grants a boon — anything but her husband's life. For the fourth boon Savitri asks for a hundred sons, "begotten by both of us". Yama agrees and walks into a trap: "Thou thyself hast bestowed on me the boon, namely, of a century of sons; yet thou takest away my husband!… May Satyavan be restored to life, for by that thy words will be made true." The King of Dharma cannot break the law, and "with cheerful heart" he unties his noose.

Nobody tricked Death: it was bound by its own word, given to The Empress's wish. **The entry of the tail turns out to be the key to its middle.** When something ends, what holds is not the attempt to keep everything as it was, but the shared wish said aloud: this is what we are growing, and it needs both of us. A wish one partner carries in silence holds no one.

Satyavan, whose name means "the one who has truth", tells the ascetics that his head ached, he fell into a deep sleep, and "there is no other reason". Without one false word, he does not know the main point of his own story. This is the minus of The Sun: one partner learns about a debt, a redundancy, the parents' decision — and "sorts it out alone". The other finds out later, from outsiders. The story of the rescue belongs to one; the rescued gets the role of a child protected from the truth.

Savitri has a formula of her own: a thing is first settled in the mind, then expressed in words, then carried out in practice. With the prophecy she skipped the middle step — the word. The main task of the tail is exactly that word. In the tale it is spoken by the fire, in front of everyone: "I have no secret to keep. Listen to the truth then!" And the Sun rises after the truth, not before.

The strong version of the tail is the way back through the night forest. Savitri places her husband's arm on her shoulder and carries his axe. He says: "By virtue of habit, the (forest) paths are known to me. And further, by the light of the moon between the trees, I can see them." She has the strength, he has the knowledge of the road, and neither leads the other all the way.

What changes the script: bad news on the same day, even in a single sentence; the one who protects asking whether the other wants to know, instead of deciding for them; a shared success told in two voices; saying aloud what is ending and what stays. In a couple, the role of Savitri goes to whoever found out first, and gender decides nothing here.

unit.title: Wake each other up

captions.M: To want a home where everything grows and all are fed
captions.N: To go through endings together, not part in silence
captions.D: To tell the truth in time, not rescue each other in secret

unit.meaning: Your task is not to rescue each other in silence: say hard things the same day and go through endings together.
